answer:
In every December entry of Samuel Pepys’ diary from 1660 up through 1667 (and again after 1669) he repeatedly mentions the same naval figure: **Admiral (later 1st Earl of Sandwich) Edward Montagu**.  
For example, on 5 December 1660 Pepys writes, “From thence to **Mr. Will. Montagu’s** chamber…”, and similar references to Montagu appear in the December entries for 1661, 1662, 1663, 1664, 1665, 1666, 1667 and 1669.  

In the December 1668 diary entry there is no mention of Edward Montagu, making him the naval figure noted in every December except that month.  

**Answer:** Admiral Edward Montagu, the future 1st Earl of Sandwich.

# Diary entries from December 1660

# [Saturday 1 December 1660](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/01/)

This morning, observing some things to be laid up not as they should be by [the girl](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/149/), I took a broom and basted her till she cried extremely, which made me vexed, but before I went out I left her appeased. So to [Whitehall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), where I found [Mr. Moore](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/340/) attending for me at [the Privy Seal](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/900/), but nothing to do to-day.

I went to my [Lord St. Albans](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1618/) lodgings, and found him in bed, talking to a priest (he looked like one) that leaned along over the side of the bed, and there I desired to know his mind about making the [catch](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9392/) stay longer, which I got ready for him the other day. He seems to be a fine civil gentleman.

To [my Lord’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), and did give up my audit of his accounts, which I had been then two days about, and was well received by my Lord. I dined with my Lord and [Lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/), and we had a [venison pasty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/384/). [Mr. Shepley](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/118/) and I went into London, and calling upon [Mr. Pinkney](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1641/), the goldsmith, he took us to the tavern, and gave us a pint of [wine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/), and there fell into our company old [Mr. Flower](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13978/) and another gentleman; who tell us how a Scotch knight was killed basely the other day at [the Fleece](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1642/) in [Covent Garden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/126/), where there had been a great many formerly killed. So to [Paul’s Churchyard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/182/), and there I took the little man at [Mr. Kirton’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1539/) and [Mr. Shepley](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/118/) to Ringstead’s at [the Star](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1643/), and after a pint of wine I went [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), my brains somewhat troubled with so much wine, and after a letter or two by the post I went to bed.

# [Sunday 2 December 1660](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/02/)

(Lord’s day). My head not very well, and my body out of order by last night’s drinking, which is my great folly. To [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), and [Mr. Mills](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1215/) made a good sermon; so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner. [My wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and I all alone to a leg of [mutton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1740/), the sawce of which being made sweet, I was angry at it, and eat none, but only dined upon the marrow bone that we had beside.

To church in the afternoon, and after sermon took [Tom Fuller’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/806/)[Church History](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1752/) and read over [Henry the 8th’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5978/) life in it, and so to supper and to bed.

# [Monday 3 December 1660](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/03/)

This morning I took a resolution to rise early in the morning, and so I rose by candle, which I have not done all this winter, and spent my morning in fiddling till time to go to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where [Sir G. Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/) did begin again discourse on [Mr. Holland’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5096/)[1](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/#fn1-1660-12-03) proposition, which [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) do take very ill, and so Sir George in lieu of that do propose that the seamen should have half in ready money and [tickets](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4086/) for the other half, to be paid in three months after, which we judge to be very practicable. After office [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, where come in my cozen [Snow](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1287/) by chance, and I had a very good [capon](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13792/) to dinner. So to the office till night, and so home, and then come [Mr. Davis](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1560/), of [Deptford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1350/) (the first time that ever he was at my house), and after him [Mons. L’Impertinent](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/170/), who is to go to Ireland to-morrow, and so came to take his leave of me. They both found me under the barber’s hand; but I had a bottle of good [sack](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/) in the house, and so made them very welcome.

Mr. Davis sat with me a good while after the other was gone, talking of his hard usage and of the endeavour to put him out of his place in the time of the late [Commissioners](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/920/), and he do speak very highly of their corruption.

After he was gone I fell a reading [‘Cornelianum dolium’](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13972/) till 11 o’clock at night with great pleasure, and after that to bed.

# [Tuesday 4 December 1660](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/04/)

To [Whitehall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) to [Sir G. Carteret’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/) chamber, where all the [officers](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1121/) met, and so we went up to [the Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/), and he took us into his closet, and we did open to him our project of stopping the growing charge of the fleet by paying them in hand one moyety, and the other four months hence. This he do like, and we returned by his order to Sir G. Carteret’s chamber, and there we did draw up this design in order to be presented to [the Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/). From thence I to [my Lord’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), and dined with him and told him what we had done to-day. [Sir Tho. Crew](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/773/) dined with my Lord to-day, and we were very merry with [Mrs. Borfett](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1651/), who dined there still as she has always done lately. After dinner Sir Tho. and [my Lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/) to [the Playhouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1611/) to see [“The Silent Woman.”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5429/) I home by water, and with [Mr. Hater](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1026/) in my chamber all alone he and I did put this morning’s design into order, which being done I did carry it to [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/), where I found some gentlemen with him ([Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) among the rest pretty merry with drink) playing at [cards](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/797/), and there I staid looking upon them till one o’clock in the morning, and so Sir W. Pen and I went away, and I to bed. This day the Parliament voted that the bodies of [Oliver](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/796/), [Ireton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2183/), [Bradshaw](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2184/), &c.,[1](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/#fn1-1660-12-04) should be taken up out of their graves in [the Abbey](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1012/), and drawn to the gallows, and there hanged and buried under it: which (methinks) do trouble me that a man of so great courage as he was, should have that dishonour, though otherwise he might deserve it enough.

# [Wednesday 5 December 1660](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/05/)

This morning the Proposal which I wrote the last night I showed to [the officers](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1121/) this morning, and was well liked of, and I wrote it fair for [Sir. G. Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/) to show to [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/), and so it is to go to the [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/).

I dined at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and after dinner I went to [the new Theatre](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1611/) and there I saw [“The Merry Wives of Windsor”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5443/) acted, the humours of the country gentleman and the French doctor very well done, but the rest but very poorly, and Sir J. Falstaffe as bad as any.

From thence to [Mr. Will. Montagu’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/563/) chamber to have sealed some writings tonight between [Sir R. Parkhurst](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1660/) and myself about [my Lord’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) 2000 _l._, but he not coming, I went to [my father’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/154/) and there found [my mother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/282/) still ill of [the stone](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/346/), and had just newly voided one, which she had let drop into the chimney, and looked and found it to shew it me.[1](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/#fn1-1660-12-05) From thence home and to bed.

# [Thursday 6 December 1660](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/06/)

This morning some of the Commissioners of [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/) and [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) went to [Sir G. Carteret’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/) office here in town, and paid off the [Chesnut](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13979/).[?? D.W.] I carried [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) to [White Friars](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1022/) and landed her there, and myself to [Whitehall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) to the [Privy Seal](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/900/), where abundance of pardons to seal, but I was much troubled for it because that there are no fees now coming for them to me. Thence [Mr. Moore](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/340/) and I alone to [the Leg](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/398/) in [King Street](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/195/), and dined together on a [neat’s tongue](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1662/) and udder.

From thence by coach to [Mr. Crew’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/105/) to [my Lord](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), who told me of his going out of town to-morrow to settle the militia in Huntingdonshire, and did desire me to lay up a box of some rich jewels and things that there are in it, which I promised to do. After much free discourse with my Lord, who tells me his mind as to his enlarging his family, &c., and desiring me to look him out a Master of the Horse and other servants, we parted. From thence I walked to [Greatorex](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/140/) (he was not within), but there I met with [Mr. Jonas Moore](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1663/), and took him to [the Five Bells](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1664/), and drank a glass of [wine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/) and left him. To [the Temple](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/131/), when [Sir R. Parkhurst](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1660/) (as was intended the last night) did seal the writings, and is to have the 2000 _l._ told to-morrow.

From, thence by water to [Parliament Stairs](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1665/), and there at an alehouse to [Doling](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/570/) (who is suddenly to go into Ireland to venture his fortune); [Simonds](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/916/) (who is at a great loss for 200 _l._ present money, which I was loth to let him have, though I could now do it, and do love him and think him honest and sufficient, yet lothness to part with money did dissuade me from it); [Luellin](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/506/) (who was very drowsy from a dose that he had got the last night), [Mr. Mount](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/571/) and several others, among the rest one [Mr. Pierce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1666/), an army man, who did make us the best sport for songs and stories in a Scotch tone (which he do very well) that ever I heard in my life. I never knew so good a companion in all my observation.

From thence to [the bridge](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/244/) by water, it being a most pleasant moonshine night, with a waterman who did tell such a company of bawdy stories, how once he carried a lady from [Putney](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1667/) in such a night as this, and she bade him lie down by her, which he did, and did give her content, and a great deal more roguery.

Home and found [my girl](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/149/) knocking at the door (it being 11 o’clock at night), her mistress having sent her out for some trivial business, which did vex me when I came in, and so I took occasion to go up and to bed in a pet.

Before I went forth this morning, one came to me to give me notice that the justices of Middlesex do meet to-morrow at [Hicks Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1668/), and that I as one am desired to be there, but I fear I cannot be there though I much desire it.

# [Friday 7 December 1660](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/07/)

This morning the judge [Advocate Fowler](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/552/) came to see me, and he and I sat talking till it was time to go to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/). To the office and there staid till past 12 o’clock, and so I left [the Comptroller](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1269/) and [Surveyor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) and went to [Whitehall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) to [my Lord’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), where I found my Lord gone this morning to [Huntingdon](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1670/), as he told me yesterday he would. I staid and dined with [my Lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/), there being [Laud](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1671/) the page’s mother there, and dined also with us, and seemed to have been a very pretty woman and of good discourse.

Before dinner I examined Laud in his Latin and found him a very pretty boy and gone a great way in Latin.

After dinner I took a box of some things of value that my Lord had left for me to carry to [the Exchequer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/242/), which I did, and left them with my [Brother Spicer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1078/), who also had this morning paid 1000 _l._ for me by appointment to [Sir R. Parkhurst](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1660/). So to [the Privy Seal](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/900/), where I signed a deadly number of pardons, which do trouble me to get nothing by. [Home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) by water, and there was much pleased to see that my little room is likely to come to be finished soon.

I fell a-reading [Fuller’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/806/)[History of Abbys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1752/), and [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) in [Great Cyrus](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9948/) till twelve at night, and so to bed.

# [Saturday 8 December 1660](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/08/)

To [Whitehall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) to [the Privy Seal](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/900/), and thence to [Mr. Pierces](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/173/) the Surgeon to tell them that I would call by and by to go to dinner. But I going into [Westminster Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/) met with [Sir G. Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/) and [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) (who were in a great fear that we had committed a great error of 100,000 _l._ in our late account gone into [the Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/) in making it too little), and so I was fain to send order to Mr. Pierces to come to my house; and also to leave the key of the chest with [Mr. Spicer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1078/); wherein my Lord’s money is, and went along with Sir W. Pen by water to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and there with [Mr. Huchinson](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1000/) we did find that we were in no mistake. And so I went to dinner with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and Mr. and [Mrs. Pierce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/785/) the Surgeon to [Mr. Pierce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/689/), the Purser (the first time that ever I was at his house) who does live very plentifully and finely. We had a lovely [chine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1705/) of [beef](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/381/) and other good things very complete and drank a great deal of [wine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/), and her daughter played after dinner upon the [virginals](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1673/), and at night by lanthorn [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) again, and Mr. Pierce and his wife being gone home I went to bed, having drunk so much wine that my head was troubled and was not very well all night, and the wind I observed was rose exceedingly before I went to bed.

# [Sunday 9 December 1660](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/09/)

(Lord’s day). Being called up early by [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) I rose and went to his house and he told me the ill news that he had this morning from [Woolwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1675/), that [the Assurance](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1726/) (formerly [Captain Holland’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/496/) ship, and now [Captain Stoakes’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/632/), designed for [Guiny](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6917/) and manned and victualled), was by a gust of wind sunk down to the bottom. Twenty men drowned. Sir Williams [both](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) went by barge thither to see how things are, and I am sent to the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) to tell him, and by boat with some other company going to [Whitehall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) from [the Old Swan](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1326/). I went to the Duke. And first calling upon [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) at his chamber, I went to the Duke’s bed-side, who had sat up late last night, and lay long this morning, who was much surprised, therewith.

This being done I went to chappell, and sat in [Mr. Blagrave’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/539/) pew, and there did sing my part along with another before [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/), and with much ease.

From thence going to [my Lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/) I met with a letter from [my Lord](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) (which Andrew had been at my house to bring me and missed me), commanding me to go to [Mr. Denham](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1676/), to get a man to go to him to-morrow to [Hinchinbroke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/104/), to contrive with him about some alterations in his house, which I did and got [Mr. Kennard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1677/).

Dined with my Lady and staid all the afternoon with her, and had infinite of talk of all kind of things, especially of beauty of men and women, with which she seems to be much pleased to talk of.

From thence at night to Mr. Kennard and took him to Mr. Denham, the Surveyor’s. Where, while we could not speak with him, his chief man ([Mr. Cooper](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1678/)) did give us a cup of good [sack](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/). From thence with Mr. Kennard to my Lady who is much pleased with him, and after a glass of sack there; we parted, having taken order for a horse or two for him and his servant to be gone to-morrow.

So to [my father’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/154/), where I sat while they were at supper, and I found [my mother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/282/) below stairs and pretty well.

Thence home, where I hear that [the Comptroller](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1269/) had some business with me, and (with [Giffin’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1529/) lanthorn) I went to him and there staid in discourse an hour ‘till late, and among other things he showed me a design of his, by the King’s making an Order of Knights of the Seal to give an encouragement for persons of honour to undertake the service of the sea, and he had done it with great pains and very ingeniously.

So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) and to prayers and to bed.

# [Monday 10 December 1660](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/10/)

Up exceedingly early to go to [the Comptroller](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1269/), but he not being up and it being a very fine, bright, moonshine morning I went and walked all alone twenty turns in [Cornhill](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1608/), from [Gracious Street](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5645/) corner to the Stockes and back again, from 6 o’clock till past 7, so long that I was weary, and going to the Comptroller’s thinking to find him ready, I found him gone, at which I was troubled, and being weary went home, and from thence with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) by water to Westminster, and put her to my father [Bowyer’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/521/) (they being newly come out of the country), but I could not stay there, but left her there. I to [the Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/) and there met with [Col. Slingsby](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1269/). So hearing that [the Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) is gone down this morning, to see [the ship](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1726/) sunk yesterday at [Woolwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1675/), he and I returned by his coach to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and after that to dinner. After dinner he came to me again and sat with me at [my house](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and among other discourse he told me that it is expected that the Duke will marry [the Lord Chancellor’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/)[daughter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1402/) at last which is likely to be the ruin of [Mr. Davis](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1528/) and my [Lord Barkley](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1055/), who have carried themselves so high against the Chancellor; [Sir Chas. Barkley](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1686/) swearing that he and others had lain with her often, which all believe to be a lie.

He and I in the evening to the [Coffee House](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/813/) in [Cornhill](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1608/), the first time that ever I was there, and I found much pleasure in it, through the diversity of company and discourse.

Home and found my wife at my [Lady Batten’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1572/), and have made a bargain to go see the ship sunk at Woolwich, where both the [Sir](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/)[Williams](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) are still since yesterday, and I do resolve to go along with them. From thence home and up to bed, having first been into my study, and to ease my mind did go to cast up how my cash stands, and I do find as near as I can that I am worth in money [clear 240 _l._](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9548/), for which God be praised.

This afternoon there was a couple of men with me with a book in each of their hands, demanding money for [pollmoney](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13946/),[1](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/#fn1-1660-12-10) and I overlooked the book and saw myself set down Samuel Pepys, gent. 10 _s._ for himself and for his servants 2 _s._, which I did presently pay without any dispute, but I fear I have not escaped so, and therefore I have long ago laid by 10 _l._ for them, but I think I am not bound to discover myself.

# [Tuesday 11 December 1660](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/11/)

[My wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and I up very early this day, and though the weather was very bad and the wind high, yet my [Lady Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1572/) and her maid and we two did go by our barge to [Woolwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1675/) (my Lady being very fearfull) where we found both [Sir](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/)[Williams](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) and much other company, expecting the weather to be better, that they might go about weighing up [the Assurance](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1726/), which lies there (poor ship, that I have been twice merry in, in [Captn. Holland’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/496/) time,) under water, only the upper deck may be seen and the masts. [Captain Stoakes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/632/) is very melancholy, and being in search for some clothes and money of his, which he says he hath lost out of his cabin. I did the first office of a justice of Peace to examine a seaman thereupon, but could find no reason to commit him.

This last tide the [Kingsale](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5269/) was also run aboard and lost her mainmast, by another ship, which makes us think it ominous to the [Guiny](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6917/) voyage, to have two of her ships spoilt before they go out.

After dinner, my Lady being very fearfull she staid and kept my wife there, and I and another gentleman, a friend of [Sir W. Pen’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/), went back in the barge, very merry by the way, as far as [Whitehall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) in her. To the [Privy Seal](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/900/), where I signed many pardons and some few things else. From thence [Mr. Moore](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/340/) and I into London to a tavern near [my house](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and there we drank and discoursed of ways how to put out a little money to the best advantage, and at present he has persuaded me to put out 250 _l._ for 50 _l._ per annum for eight years, and I think I shall do it.

Thence home, where I found [the wench](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/149/) washing, and I up to my study, and there did make up an even 100 _l._, and sealed it to lie by. After that to bed.

From thence up with [J. Thence [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and took out this 100 _l._ and sealed it up with the other last night, it being the first 200 _l._ that ever I saw together of my own in my life. For which God be praised.

So to my [Lady Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1572/), and sat an hour or two, and talked with her daughter and people in the absence of [her father](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) and mother and my wife to pass away the time. After that home and to bed, reading myself asleep, while [the wench](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/149/) sat mending my breeches by my bedside.

In the morning to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), and then dined at home. Thence to [my Lady’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/) and staid with her an hour or two talking of [the Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) and [his lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1402/), [the Chancellor’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/)[daughter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1402/), between whom, she tells me, that all is agreed and he will marry her. It rained hard, and my Lady would have had me have the coach, but I would not, but to [my father’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/154/), where I met [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), and there supped, and after supper by [link](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1167/)[home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) and to bed.

Batten’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) to dinner, where much and good company. My wife not very well went home, I staid late there seeing them play at [cards](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/797/), and so home to bed.

This afternoon there came in a strange lord to Sir William Batten’s by a mistake and enters discourse with him, so that we could not be rid of him till [Sir Arn. Breames](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1587/) and [Mr. Bens](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1745/) and [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) fell a-drinking to him till he was drunk, and so sent him away. About the middle of the night I was very ill — I think with eating and drinking too much — and so I was forced to call [the maid](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/149/), who pleased my wife and I in her running up and down so innocently in her smock, and vomited in the bason, and so to sleep, and in the morning was pretty well, only got cold, and so had pain … [in pissing – L&M] as I used to have.

# [Friday 28 December 1660](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/28/)

Office day. There all the morning. Dined at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) alone with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), and so staid within all the afternoon and evening; at my [lute](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/540/), with great pleasure, and so to bed with great content.

# [Saturday 29 December 1660](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/29/)

Within all the morning. Several people to speak with me; [Mr. Shepley](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/118/) for 100 _l._; [Mr. Kennard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1677/) and [Warren](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1748/), the merchant, about [deals](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4992/) for [my Lord](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/). [Captain Robert Blake](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/663/) lately come from [the Straights](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3260/) about some Florence [Wine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/) for my Lord, and with him I went to [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/), who offering me a barrel of [oysters](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/373/) I took them both [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to my house (having by chance a good piece of roast [beef](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/381/) at the fire for dinner), and there they dined with me, and sat talking all the afternoon-good company. Thence to [Alderman Backwell’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/967/) and took a brave state-plate and cupp in lieu of the candlesticks that I had the other day and carried them by coach to my Lord’s and left them there. And so back to [my father’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/154/) and saw [my mother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/282/), and so to my [uncle Fenner’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/749/), whither my father came to me, and there we talked and drank, and so away; I home with my father, he telling me what bad wives both my [cozen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1105/)[Joyces](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1749/) make to [their](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1107/)[husbands](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1090/), which I much wondered at. After talking of [my sister’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1568/) coming to me next week, I went home and to bed.

# [Sunday 30 December 1660](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/30/)

(Lord’s day). Lay long in bed, and being up, I went with [Will](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1082/) to [my Lord’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), calling in at many churches in my way. There I found [Mr. Shepley](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/118/), in his Venetian cap, taking physique in his chamber, and with him I sat till dinner.

My Lord dined abroad and [my Lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/) in her chamber, so [Mr. Hetly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/858/), [Child](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1253/) and I dined together, and after dinner Mr. Child and I spent some time at the [lute](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/540/), and so promising to prick me some lessons to my [theorbo](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/457/) he went away to see [Henry Laws](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/866/), who lies very sick.

I to [the Abby](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1012/) and walked there, seeing the great confusion of people that come there to hear the [organs](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1586/). So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), calling in at [my father’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/154/), but staid not, my father and [mother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/282/) being both forth.

At home I fell a-reading of [Fuller’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/806/)[Church History](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1752/) till it was late, and so to bed.

# [Monday 31 December 1660](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/31/)

At [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) all the morning and after that [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and not staying to dine I went out, and in [Paul’s Church-yard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/182/) I bought the play of [“Henry the Fourth,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5442/) and so went to [the new Theatre](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1611/) (only calling at [Mr. Crew’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/105/) and eat a bit with the people there at dinner) and saw it acted; but my expectation being too great, it did not please me, as otherwise I believe it would; and my having a book, I believe did spoil it a little.

That being done I went to [my Lord’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), where I found him private at [cards](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/797/) with my [Lord Lauderdale](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/767/) and some persons of honour. So [Mr. Shepley](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/118/) and I over to [Harper’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/241/), and there drank a pot or two, and so parted. [My boy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1248/) taking a cat home with him from my Lord’s, which [Sarah](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5611/) had given him for [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), we being much troubled with mice.

At [Whitehall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) inquiring for a coach, there was a Frenchman with one eye that was going my way, so he and I hired the coach between us and he set me down in [Fenchurch Street](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1075/). Strange how the fellow, without asking, did tell me all what he was, and how he had ran away from his father and come into England to serve [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/), and now going back again.

Home and to bed.

**George Monck, 1st Duke of Albemarle** (6 December 1608 – 3 January 1670) was a professional soldier from [Devon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devon "Devon") who fought on both sides during the [Wars of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Wars of the Three Kingdoms"). A prominent military figure under the [Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England "Commonwealth of England"), his support was crucial to the 1660 [Stuart Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration") of [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England").

Monck began his military career in 1625 and served in the [Eighty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighty_Years%27_War "Eighty Years' War") until 1638, when he returned to England. Posted to [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland") as part of the army sent to suppress the [Irish Rebellion of 1641](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Rebellion_of_1641 "Irish Rebellion of 1641"), he quickly gained a reputation for efficiency and ruthlessness. After [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") agreed to a truce with the [Catholic Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_Ireland "Confederate Ireland") in September 1643, he was captured fighting for the [Royalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier") at [Nantwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Nantwich "Battle of Nantwich") in January 1644 and remained a prisoner for the next two years.

Released in 1647, he was named [Parliamentarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") commander in Eastern [Ulster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster "Ulster"), fought in Scotland under [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") in the 1650 to 1652 [Anglo-Scottish War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Scottish_war_(1650%E2%80%931652) "Anglo-Scottish war (1650–1652)"), and served as [General at sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_at_sea "General at sea") during the 1652 to 1654 [First Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Dutch_War "First Anglo-Dutch War"). From 1655 to 1660, he was army commander in Scotland, and his support for moderates in [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England") who wanted to restore the monarchy proved decisive in Charles II regaining his throne in May 1660.

Monck was rewarded by being made [Duke of Albemarle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Albemarle "Duke of Albemarle") and given various senior positions. Illness and lack of interest in politics meant he faded into the background after 1660, but returned to sea during the [Second Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Dutch_War "Second Anglo-Dutch War"). He played an important leadership role during the 1665 [Great Plague of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plague_of_London "Great Plague of London"), as well as the 1666 [Great Fire of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London "Great Fire of London"), and died in January 1670.

## Personal details

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/GreatPotheridge_Merton_Devon.JPG/250px-GreatPotheridge_Merton_Devon.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GreatPotheridge_Merton_Devon.JPG)

Great Potheridge in 2014, the surviving wing of Monck's family home

Monck was born 6 December 1608 on the family estate of [Potheridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potheridge "Potheridge") in [Devon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devon "Devon"), second son of Sir [Thomas Monck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Monck "Thomas Monck") (1570–1627) and Elizabeth Smith, whose father Sir [George Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Smith_(MP_for_Exeter) "George Smith (MP for Exeter)") was reputedly the richest man in [Exeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exeter "Exeter"), and three times [Mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Exeter "Mayor of Exeter").[[1]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYerbyHunneyball2010-1) Monck's younger brother [Nicholas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Monck "Nicholas Monck") (1609–1661) became [Bishop of Hereford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Hereford "Bishop of Hereford") and [Provost of Eton College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_provosts_of_Eton_College "List of provosts of Eton College"), while his elder brother Thomas died in 1647.[[2]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWestminster_Abbey-2) Monck was a descendant of [Arthur Plantagenet, 1st Viscount Lisle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Plantagenet,_1st_Viscount_Lisle "Arthur Plantagenet, 1st Viscount Lisle"), due to a marriage between Thomas Monke and Frances Plantagenet, and thus also an illegitimate [cognatic descendant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognatic_kinship "Cognatic kinship") of [Edward IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_IV "Edward IV").[[3]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-3)

Despite being one of the oldest families in Devon, the Moncks were relatively poor, while Smith allegedly failed to pay his daughter's [dowry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dowry "Dowry"), leading to a series of expensive legal disputes with his son-in-law.[[4]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStoyle1993-4) In 1625, Sir Thomas was imprisoned for debt and died in jail two years later.[[5]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunneyball2010-5)

In January 1653, Monck married Anne Clarges (1619–1670), daughter of a London [farrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farrier "Farrier") and widow of Thomas Radford, whose death was not legally confirmed until a year after their marriage, a fact later used against her.[[6]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen1979100-6) Anne allegedly had strong [Royalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier") sympathies like her brother [Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Clarges "Thomas Clarges") (1618–1695), who was knighted after the [Stuart Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration") and had a long career in [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England").[[7]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHelmsNaylor1983-7) They had one son who survived into adulthood, [Christopher Monck, 2nd Duke of Albemarle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Monck,_2nd_Duke_of_Albemarle "Christopher Monck, 2nd Duke of Albemarle") (1653–1688).[[8]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHutton2004-8)

## Early career, pre-1641

Monck became a professional soldier, a common career choice for younger sons of impoverished gentry. His first experience was the failed attack on [Cádiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A1diz_expedition_(1625) "Cádiz expedition (1625)") in November 1625, when he served as an [ensign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensign_(rank) "Ensign (rank)") in a company commanded by his cousin [Sir Richard Grenville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Richard_Grenville,_1st_Baronet "Sir Richard Grenville, 1st Baronet"). He later joined the equally disastrous expedition against [St Martin-de-Ré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Saint-Martin-de-R%C3%A9 "Siege of Saint-Martin-de-Ré") in July 1627; it is suggested one reason for doing so was his arrest for attempted murder in late 1626, when he and his brother Thomas assaulted Nicholas Battyn, the [undersheriff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undersheriff "Undersheriff") responsible for jailing their father.[[4]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStoyle1993-4)

He spent most of the next decade serving in the [Dutch States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_States_Army "Dutch States Army"), which was then considered the best place to learn the 'art of war' due to its success in the [Eighty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighty_Years%27_War "Eighty Years' War") against [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habsburg_Spain "Habsburg Spain"). Many officers who later fought on both sides during the [Wars of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Wars of the Three Kingdoms") did the same, among them Sir [Thomas Fairfax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Fairfax "Thomas Fairfax") and Sir [Philip Skippon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Skippon "Philip Skippon").[[9]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunthorne2017176-9) During the [capture of Maastricht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Maastricht "Capture of Maastricht") in 1632, he served in a regiment commanded by the [Earl of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_de_Vere,_19th_Earl_of_Oxford "Robert de Vere, 19th Earl of Oxford"), who was killed in the final assault and replaced by [George Goring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Goring,_Lord_Goring "George Goring, Lord Goring"). By 1637, Monck was [lieutenant colonel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_colonel "Lieutenant colonel") under Goring and played a decisive role in storming [Breda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Breda_(1637) "Siege of Breda (1637)"), a Dutch success which was one of the last major actions of the war. After quarrelling with the civil authorities of [Dordrecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dordrecht "Dordrecht"), he surrendered his commission and returned to England in 1638.[[8]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHutton2004-8)

During the 1639 and 1640 [Bishops' Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops%27_Wars "Bishops' Wars"), he was lieutenant colonel in a regiment raised by [Mountjoy Blount, 1st Earl of Newport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountjoy_Blount,_1st_Earl_of_Newport "Mountjoy Blount, 1st Earl of Newport"), who was also [Master-General of the Ordnance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master-General_of_the_Ordnance "Master-General of the Ordnance"). Monck was one of the few to emerge with any credit from the [Battle of Newburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Newburn "Battle of Newburn") in 1640, when he saved the English artillery from capture. Lack of money meant the army was dissolved. Monck spent the next year unemployed.[[8]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHutton2004-8)

## Ireland and England, 1641–1646

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/James_Butler%2C_1st_Duke_of_Ormonde_by_Sir_Peter_Lely.jpg/250px-James_Butler%2C_1st_Duke_of_Ormonde_by_Sir_Peter_Lely.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:James_Butler,_1st_Duke_of_Ormonde_by_Sir_Peter_Lely.jpg)

The [Earl of Ormond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Butler,_1st_Duke_of_Ormond "James Butler, 1st Duke of Ormond"), Royalist commander who dominated Irish politics for much of the 17th century

Following the [Irish Rebellion of 1641](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Rebellion_of_1641 "Irish Rebellion of 1641"), [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England") approved the recruitment of a [Royal Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Royal_Army "Irish Royal Army") to suppress it. Monck was made colonel of a regiment raised by his distant relative [Robert Sidney, 2nd Earl of Leicester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Sidney,_2nd_Earl_of_Leicester "Robert Sidney, 2nd Earl of Leicester"), which landed in [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin") in January 1642 and served under the [Earl of Ormond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Butler,_1st_Duke_of_Ormond "James Butler, 1st Duke of Ormond").[[8]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHutton2004-8) Over the next eighteen months, he campaigned against rebel strongholds in [Leinster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leinster "Leinster"), during which he was responsible for several alleged massacres in [County Kildare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Kildare "County Kildare") and also took part in the March 1643 [Battle of New Ross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_New_Ross_(1643) "Battle of New Ross (1643)").[[10]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClavin2009-10) However, the outbreak of the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War") in August 1642 meant Ormonde could no longer receive reinforcements or money from England, and by mid-1643, the [Catholic Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_Ireland "Confederate Ireland") controlled most of Ireland, with the exception of [Ulster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster "Ulster"), [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin") and [Cork City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cork_City "Cork City").[[11]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBCW-11)

Most of Ormond's officers, including Monck, argued the Irish Army should remain neutral between [Parliamentarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") and [Royalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier") but Charles was anxious to use these troops to help him win the war in England and in September 1643, Ormonde agreed a truce or "Cessation" with the Confederacy. Factions on both sides objected to the terms, which included negotiations on freedom of worship for Catholics and constitutional reforms. Protestants saw this as a threat, while many Confederates felt they were on the verge of victory and gained nothing from the truce; they were also well aware any concessions Charles made to Catholics in Ireland undermined his position in England and Scotland.[[12]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2006211%E2%80%93212-12)

Monck was among those who refused to swear allegiance to the king and was sent by Ormonde as a prisoner to [Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol "Bristol"), where he eventually agreed to support the Royalists before being captured at [Nantwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Nantwich "Battle of Nantwich") in January 1644. Although prisoners were commonly exchanged, his experience and ability were so highly regarded that he remained in custody for the next two years, during which he wrote a military manual entitled _Observations on Military and Political Affairs_. Following Charles's surrender in May 1646, he accepted an appointment in one of the regiments sent to Ireland by Parliament as reinforcements; in September 1647, he was appointed Parliamentarian commander in Eastern Ulster.[[8]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHutton2004-8)

## The Interregnum

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/Oliver_Cromwell_by_Robert_Walker.jpg/250px-Oliver_Cromwell_by_Robert_Walker.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Oliver_Cromwell_by_Robert_Walker.jpg)

_[Portrait of Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait\_of\_Oliver\_Cromwell "Portrait of Oliver Cromwell")_ by [Robert Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Walker_(painter) "Robert Walker (painter)"), 1649. Monck's support for the [Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Protectorate "The Protectorate") was based on his personal regard for its leader.

Monck proved his loyalty to Parliament by refusing to take part in the [Second English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War "Second English Civil War") and requiring all his officers to sign a declaration of support. However, his position in Ulster became extremely precarious following the [execution of Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Execution_of_Charles_I "Execution of Charles I") in January 1649, since it was dominated by [Scots Presbyterian settlers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster_Protestants "Ulster Protestants"), supported by a [Covenanter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanter "Covenanter") army under [Robert Monro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Monro "Robert Monro").[[13]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWedgwood200182%E2%80%9383-13) The Scots did not only object to the English killing their king without consultation. As [Calvinists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinist "Calvinist"), they viewed monarchy as divinely ordained, making the execution [sacrilegious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacrilegious "Sacrilegious").[[14]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacleod20095%E2%80%9319_passim-14) As a result, they defected to the Royalist–Confederate alliance led by Ormond and in desperation, Monck agreed to a secret truce with [Eoghan Ó Néill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Roe_O%27Neill "Owen Roe O'Neill"), the Catholic leader in Ulster, which he did not communicate to Parliament until May.[[10]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClavin2009-10)

Recalled to London, he was reprimanded by a Parliamentary committee, although they privately recognised the desperate circumstances which made it necessary. Although some mistrusted Monck as a former Royalist, [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") gave him command of a regiment in the 1650 to 1651 [Anglo-Scottish War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Scottish_war_(1650%E2%80%931652) "Anglo-Scottish war (1650–1652)"), which fought at [Dunbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dunbar_(1650) "Battle of Dunbar (1650)"), then [stormed Dundee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Dundee "Siege of Dundee"), an action in which 800 civilians were allegedly killed.[[15]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeneral_George_Monck's_Regiment-15) Throughout the [Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Protectorate "The Protectorate"), Monck remained loyal to Cromwell, who appointed him military commander in Scotland until February 1652. At that time, Monck became seriously ill and retired to [Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath,_Somerset "Bath, Somerset") in order to recover. Due to his expertise in utilising artillery, when the [First Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Dutch_War "First Anglo-Dutch War") began in November, Monck was made a [General at Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_at_Sea "General at Sea"), along with [Robert Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Blake_(admiral) "Robert Blake (admiral)") and [Richard Deane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Deane_(regicide) "Richard Deane (regicide)"). He fought in the 1653 naval battles of [Portland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Portland "Battle of Portland"), [the Gabbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Gabbard "Battle of the Gabbard") and [Scheveningen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Scheveningen "Battle of Scheveningen").[[8]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHutton2004-8)

In April 1653, Cromwell dissolved the [Rump Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rump_Parliament "Rump Parliament") and in June Monck was nominated [MP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)") for [Devon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devon_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Devon (UK Parliament constituency)") in [Barebone's Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barebone%27s_Parliament "Barebone's Parliament").[[16]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHelmsFerris1983-16) Although the Dutch war did not formally end until the February 1654 [Treaty of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Westminster_(1654) "Treaty of Westminster (1654)"), Monck was recalled and sent to Scotland to suppress the Royalist [Glencairn's rising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glencairn%27s_rising "Glencairn's rising"). Appointed military commander, he employed the ruthless tactics demonstrated in his previous assignments and by the end of 1655 the country had been [pacified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacification_(military_action) "Pacification (military action)"). He retained this position for the next five years, demonstrating his loyalty by removing any officers who expressed opposition to government policy and arresting religious dissidents.[[8]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHutton2004-8)

## The Restoration

When Oliver Cromwell died in September 1658, Monck transferred his support to his son [Richard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell"), who was appointed [Lord Protector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Protector "Lord Protector"). The [Third Protectorate Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Protectorate_Parliament "Third Protectorate Parliament") elected in January 1659 was dominated by moderate Presbyterians like Monck and Royalist sympathisers, whose main objective was to reduce the power and expense of the military. In April, army radicals led by [John Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lambert_(general) "John Lambert (general)") and [Charles Fleetwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Fleetwood "Charles Fleetwood") dissolved Parliament and forced the resignation of Richard Cromwell. Sometimes known as the [Wallingford House party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallingford_House_party "Wallingford House party"), the new regime abolished the Protectorate, reseated the [Rump Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rump_Parliament "Rump Parliament") dismissed by Cromwell in 1653 and began removing officers and officials of suspect loyalty, including many of those serving in Scotland.[[17]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWorden201082%E2%80%9383-17)

Monck was left in place largely because rumours of another Royalist rising made it preferable to retain him. Both his cousin [John Grenville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Granville,_1st_Earl_of_Bath "John Granville, 1st Earl of Bath") and brother Nicholas were connected with the [Royalist underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sealed_Knot "Sealed Knot") and in July 1659, Nicholas brought him a personal appeal from [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England"), asking for his help and offering up to £100,000 per year for his assistance.[[18]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJordanWalsh2012126-18) When [Booth's Uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booth%27s_Uprising "Booth's Uprising") broke out in August 1659, Monck considered joining it but the revolt collapsed before he had time to commit himself. In October, the Wallingford House group dismissed the Rump before being forced to reinstate it in early December.[[19]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHutton1989127-19)

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/The_arrival_of_King_Charles_II_of_England_in_Rotterdam%2C_may_24_1660_%28Lieve_Pietersz._Verschuier%2C_1665%29.jpg/500px-The_arrival_of_King_Charles_II_of_England_in_Rotterdam%2C_may_24_1660_%28Lieve_Pietersz._Verschuier%2C_1665%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_arrival_of_King_Charles_II_of_England_in_Rotterdam,_may_24_1660_(Lieve_Pietersz._Verschuier,_1665).jpg)

Charles leaves the Dutch Republic for England, 24 May 1660.

By the end of 1659, England appeared to be drifting into anarchy, with widespread demands for new elections and an end to military rule. Monck declared his support for the Rump against the Republican faction led by Lambert, while co-ordinating with Sir [Theophilus Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theophilus_Jones_(soldier) "Theophilus Jones (soldier)"), a former colleague in Ireland who seized [Dublin Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin_Castle "Dublin Castle") in late December.[[10]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClavin2009-10) At the same time, he marched his army to the English border, supported by a force raised by former [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army") commander Sir [Thomas Fairfax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Fairfax "Thomas Fairfax"). Outnumbered and unpaid, Lambert's troops melted away; on 2 February Monck entered London and in April elections were held for a [Convention Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_Parliament_(1660) "Convention Parliament (1660)").[[20]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris200643%E2%80%9344-20)

While his backing was essential to the [Stuart Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration"), modern historians question whether the policy was initiated by Monck as opposed to following majority opinion, which by now was overwhelmingly in favour of reinstating the monarchy.[[21]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHutton1989128-21) Although he was elected MP for Devon, observers noted that he had little interest in politics, while his lack of a regional power base in England and the proposed reduction of the army worked against his future influence.[[16]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHelmsFerris1983-16) It has also been suggested the Royalist sympathies of his wife played an important role in his decision.[[22]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeay2022-22)

Regardless of his motives, the [Declaration of Breda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_Breda "Declaration of Breda") issued by Charles on 4 April 1660 was largely based on Monck's recommendations. It promised a general pardon for actions committed during the [civil wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Wars of the Three Kingdoms") and [Interregnum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interregnum "Interregnum"), with the exception of the [regicides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_regicides_of_Charles_I "List of regicides of Charles I"), retention by the current owners of property purchased during the same period, religious toleration and payment of arrears to the army.[[23]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTESharp2000175-23) Based on these terms, Parliament resolved to proclaim Charles king and invited him to return to England; he left Holland on 24 May and entered London five days later.[[24]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHutton1989131-24)

## Later career and death

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Quartered_arms_of_George_Monck%2C_1st_Duke_of_Albemarle%2C_KG.png/250px-Quartered_arms_of_George_Monck%2C_1st_Duke_of_Albemarle%2C_KG.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Quartered_arms_of_George_Monck,_1st_Duke_of_Albemarle,_KG.png)

Quartered arms of George Monck, 1st Duke of Albemarle

In July 1660, Monck was made [Duke of Albemarle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Albemarle "Duke of Albemarle"), appointed to the [Privy Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council_of_England "Privy Council of England"), made [Lord Deputy of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Deputy_of_Ireland "Lord Deputy of Ireland") and [Lord Lieutenant of Devon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Lieutenant_of_Devon "Lord Lieutenant of Devon"). He was also given the former [Palace of Beaulieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Beaulieu "Palace of Beaulieu"), along with lands in Ireland and England worth £7,000 per year and an annual pension of £700. Among his friends and relatives, John Grenville became [Earl of Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Bath "Earl of Bath"), while Nicholas Monck was appointed Bishop of Hereford, his cousin [William Morice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Morice_(Secretary_of_State) "William Morice (Secretary of State)")[Secretary of State for the Northern Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_the_Northern_Department "Secretary of State for the Northern Department") and his brother-in-law Thomas [Commissary General of Musters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissary "Commissary").[[25]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen1979102%E2%80%93103-25)

When Monck fell seriously ill once again in August 1661, he was replaced in Ireland by Ormond, and compensated with the additional office of [Lord Lieutenant of Middlesex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Lieutenant_of_Middlesex "Lord Lieutenant of Middlesex"). Thereafter he avoided front-line politics and focused on maximising his personal wealth, his wife becoming notorious for selling offices, although this was a common practice and probably reflected resentment at her humble origins. In his diary, [Samuel Pepys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys "Samuel Pepys") attacks her as a "homely, plain dowd" and "filthy woman", although his views were almost certainly coloured by the rivalry between Monck and his own cousin [Edward Montagu, 1st Earl of Sandwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich "Edward Montagu, 1st Earl of Sandwich"), for control of the [Admiralty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admiralty_in_the_17th_century "Admiralty in the 17th century").[[26]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen1979100%E2%80%93101-26)

In 1663, Monck was allocated lands in the [Province of Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Carolina "Province of Carolina"), now the modern US states of [South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina") and [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"), whose [Albemarle Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albemarle_Sound "Albemarle Sound") is named after him.[[27]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-27) He was also made a shareholder in the [Royal African Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_African_Company "Royal African Company"), established to challenge Dutch control of the [Atlantic slave trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_slave_trade "Atlantic slave trade") and a major factor in the commercial tensions between the two countries that eventually led to the [Second Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Dutch_War "Second Anglo-Dutch War") in 1665. The conflict was backed by Monck and other investors within the government, including [George Carteret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Carteret "George Carteret"), [Shaftesbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Ashley_Cooper,_1st_Earl_of_Shaftesbury "Anthony Ashley Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury") and [Arlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Bennet,_1st_Earl_of_Arlington "Henry Bennet, 1st Earl of Arlington").[[28]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTESherman1976331%E2%80%93332-28)

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Monument_to_George_Monck_in_Westminster_Abbey.jpg/250px-Monument_to_George_Monck_in_Westminster_Abbey.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Monument_to_George_Monck_in_Westminster_Abbey.jpg)

Monument to Monck in [Westminster Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey")

Command of the fleet was given to [James, Duke of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_II_of_England "James II of England"), with Sandwich as his deputy and Monck took over his administrative duties at the Admiralty. He also gained a great deal of popularity for remaining in London throughout the 1665 [Great Plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plague_of_London "Great Plague of London") when most of the government fled to [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford "Oxford").[[29]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen1979114-29) Monck and [Prince Rupert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Rupert_of_the_Rhine "Prince Rupert of the Rhine") shared command during the 1666 campaign; the [Four Days' Battle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Days%27_Battle "Four Days' Battle") in June was a Dutch victory, offset by English success at the [St. James's Day Battle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._James%27s_Day_Battle "St. James's Day Battle") in July. In September he was recalled to help maintain order in the chaos created by the [Great Fire of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London "Great Fire of London").[[8]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHutton2004-8)

This was his last active command; the fleet had to be laid up due to lack of money, culminating in the humiliating [raid on the Medway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raid_on_the_Medway "Raid on the Medway") in June 1667 which ended the war. One of the few to escape censure by Parliament, Monck was appointed [First Lord of the Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lord_of_the_Treasury "First Lord of the Treasury") but he was now suffering from severe [oedema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oedema "Oedema") which limited his ability to attend meetings.[[16]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHelmsFerris1983-16) He died on 3 January 1670, followed three weeks later by his wife, and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey").[[2]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWestminster_Abbey-2) Some years later, a monument by [William Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kent "William Kent") and [Peter Scheemakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Scheemakers "Peter Scheemakers") was erected in the Abbey in Monck's honour.[[2]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWestminster_Abbey-2) The ballad "[On the Death of His Grace, the Duke of Albemarle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Death_of_His_Grace,_the_Duke_of_Albemarle "On the Death of His Grace, the Duke of Albemarle")" was composed in his honour.[[30]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#cite_note-30)

### [David Gurliacci](http://biblio.org/gutenberg/etext98/1hoej10.txt "Visit this person’s website")on 30 Dec 2002•[Link](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111#c35 "Link directly to this annotation")

Historian Thomas Macaulay's description of Monk:

"George Monk, was himself the very opposite of a zealot. ... He had at the commencement of the civil war, borne arms for the King, had been made prisoner by the Roundheads, had then accepted a commission from the Parliament, and, with very slender pretensions to saintship, had raised himself to high commands by his courage and professional skill. He had been an useful servant to both Protectors, and had quietly acquiesced when the officers at Westminster had pulled down Richard [Cromwell] and restord the Long Parliament, and would perhaps have acquiesced as quietly in the second expulsion of the Long Parliament, if the provisional government had abstained from giving him cause of offence and apprehension. For his nature was cautious and somewhat sluggish; nor was he at all disposed to hazard sure and moderate advantages for the chalice of obtaining even the most splendid success. He seems to have been impelled to attack the new rulers of the Commonwealth less by the hope that, if he overthrew them, he should become great, than by the fear that, if he submitted to them, he should not even be secure. Whatever were his motives, [in 1660] he declared himself the champion of the oppressed civil power, refused to acknowledge the usurped authority of the provisional government, and, at the head of seven thousand veterans, marched into England."

--From Thomas Babington Macaulay's History of England From the Accession of James II, Vol. I, Chapter 1 (1848) (text available online at Project Gutenberg)

Monk, at least in Macaulay's description, sounds something like George Washington at the tail end of the American Revolution, when unpaid and disgruntled troops started to grumble about marching on Congress, a move that could well have resulted in a dictatorship and/or some kind of royal restoration in America. Washington strongly supported Congress and prevailed over the grumblers. It isn't hard to imagine that the 18th century general knew something of the history of 1659-60.

A colorful, dismissive description of Monk is given by Henry B. Wheatley in his book, "Samuel Pepys and the World He Lived In" (1880):

"George Monk, Duke of Albemarle, was a singularly unheroic character. Anne Clarges Monck, Duchess of Albemarle's biographies in our Encyclopedia make the Duke sound like some country bumkin who sort of accidentally became the man who saved England from a fourth Civil War.

Gen. George Monck was not a country bumkin.

He was born at the manor house of Great Potheridge near Torrington, Devonshire on 6 December 1608, the fourth child and second son of Sir Thomas Monck, an impoverished landowner, and his wife Elizabeth, daughter of John Smyth, a wealthy merchant of Exeter. Her first husband was Mayor of Exeter three times and a very wealth man.

George was related to both Robert Sidney, 2nd Earl of Leicester and Sir Richard Grenville MP, another Devonshire warrior of the early 17th century. A young George Monck fought with both of these men, so he knew them.

Gen. George Monck's first cousin on his mother's side was John Grenville, 1st Earl of Bath (1628–1701), who probably owed his elevation to Monck.

However, Monck did not come to prominence through nepotism. His uncles gave him his start in the military, but he earned every accolade he received, on land and at sea, both in wartime and during times of peace.

Second sons of poor relatives often work harder than first sons of rich relatives.

Gen. George Monck is best known for the key role that he played in the Restoration of the Monarchy in 1660 when his actions undoubtedly changed the course of British history. Monck began his march into England in Jan. 1660, arriving in London just over a month later. Cooperation from Henry Fairfax, 3rd Lord Fairfax, who had agreed to join Monck in opposing a restoration of Charles Stuart, ensured that no opposition was offered by Lambert’s troops.

Monck’s opposition to a restoration was confirmed in his letter to the gentlemen of Devon, warning them that the growth of new interests, such as Dissenting sects and those who had benefited from the purchase of forfeited church and royalist lands, required the protection of a republic and therefore the continued exclusion of the secluded Members.

Yet demands for the return of the secluded MPs and for calling a free Parliament continued to grow. Many of the addresses were handed to Monck.

At Monck’s suggestion all the forces in London, except his own, were dispersed to new and scattered quarters in order to prevent any attempt at a military coup d’état. 

On 6 Feb. he addressed Parliament, choosing his words with so much care that ‘most men know not what construction to make of it’.

On Feb. 7 Pepys reported that Monck ‘hath now the absolute command and power to do anything that hath a mind to do’, but his remarks were premature, for on 9 Feb. Monck complied with an order from the Rump to take action against the City of London. 

On 11 Feb. he ordered the Rump to issue writs for fresh elections and to dissolve itself, but wrangling about the qualifications that should be imposed on candidates – and therefore the political complexion of any new Parliament – continued.

Monck then presided over several meetings between representatives of the Rump and of the secluded Members, but no agreement was reached. According to Anthony Ashley Cooper, Lord Ashley MP, on the night of 20 Feb. he, with Mrs. Monck, her brother, Thomas Clarges, John Cloberry, and Ralph Knight, sat up arguing with Monck until 3 a.m. about the need for the immediate readmission of the secluded Members. 

That Anne Monck had considerable influence over her husband and that she used it in favor of a restoration is highly probable. There were suggestions that the exiled king should make a point of encouraging her. Whether Ashley’s account is accurate is another matter.

There are indications that something may have been brewing earlier, for Pepys reported a meeting of the secluded Members with Monck on 17 Feb. and another meeting of the secluded Members on 19 Feb. at the home of John Crew, later Baron Crew, which (considering Crew’s Calvinism and it ‘being the Lord’s day’) he thought must suggest ‘something extraordinary in the business’.
